title: Combinational Logic Circuits - Gates, Minimization, MUX, Decoders, Adders
subtitle: Boolean functions, gates, K-map, MUX/DEMUX, decoders, encoders, adders, subtractors, comparators - design for functionality and timing
subtopics: Multiplexers and Demultiplexers (incl. F=Sum(0,1,3,4,6) on 4-to-1 MUX)

readingSections.title: 1. Boolean Foundations - Truth Tables, SOP, POS (From Zero)
readingSections.quickSummary: A combinational output depends only on present inputs. Truth table lists every input combo. SOP adds the rows where output is 1.
content: Combinational means no memory: same inputs always give same output. Contrast with sequential (later topic) where past matters. Every question here is a truth table in some disguise.

A truth table with $n$ inputs has $2^{n}$ rows. Write binary counting $00...0$ to $11...1$. Minterm $m_{i}$ is the AND of all inputs for row $i$ (complement where input is $0$). Maxterm $M_{i}$ is the OR. SOP (sum of products) ORs the minterms where output is $1$. POS (product of sums) ANDs the maxterms where output is $0$. Both describe the same function.
Example $2$-input XOR: rows $00\to0, 01\to1, 10\to1, 11\to0$. SOP: $F = A'B + AB'$. POS: $F = (A+B)(A'+B')$. VEDA writes $F(A,B,C) = \sum(0,1,3,4,6)$ meaning SOP minterms $0,1,3,4,6$ are $1$.

Core laws: Identity ($A+0=A, A\cdot1=A$), Null ($A+1=1, A\cdot0=0$), Idempotent ($A+A=A$), Complement ($A+A'=1, A\cdot A'=0$), Commutative, Associative, Distributive, Absorption ($A+AB=A$), Consensus ($AB+A'C+BC=AB+A'C$), De Morgan (below). Duality: swap AND/OR and $0$/$1$ to get a second theorem free.

subsections.title: SOP and POS with a worked example
content: SOP: focus on $1$-rows, AND each row, OR the rows. POS: focus on $0$-rows, OR each row, AND the rows.
Function $F(A,B) = 1$ only when $A \neq B$ (XOR): SOP $A'B + AB'$.
Notation $\sum m(1,2)$ equals $\sum(1,2)$. $\prod M(0,3)$ is the POS twin.

example.prompt: Write SOP for F=1 on rows 0 and 3 of A,B (XNOR)

subsections.title: De Morgan - the most-used law in VLSI
content: De Morgan: $\overline{A+B} = \bar{A}\cdot\bar{B}$ and $\overline{A\cdot B} = \bar{A}+\bar{B}$. Break the bar, flip the sign. Extends to $n$ variables.
Why it matters: NAND is AND+NOT, NOR is OR+NOT. De Morgan converts between them, which is how NAND-only designs (VEDA Q2) are derived and how(any AND-OR becomes NAND-NAND for CMOS.
Bubble pushing: a bubble (NOT) crossing a gate flips AND to OR. Two bubbles cancel. This visual trick simplifies transistor-level schematics.

subsections.title: Canonical vs minimal form
content: Canonical SOP lists every minterm fully (each with all literals). Minimal form is shorter after minimization (next section). Both give identical truth tables.
VEDA gives canonical $\sum(0,1,3,4,6)$ and asks for MUX or gate implementation - you choose the form that fits the hardware, not necessarily minimal SOP first.

quickRevision: n inputs give 2^n rows. SOP = OR of minterms where F=1.
De Morgan: break bar, flip AND/OR.
readingSections.companyNote: SOP/sigma notation appears verbatim in VEDA mains. Misreading it loses the whole question.

readingSections.title: 2. Logic Gates and Universal NAND/NOR (VEDA Q2 Inside)
readingSections.quickSummary: NAND alone (or NOR alone) can build any function. A 4-input NAND needs five 2-input NANDs by cascade or tree.
content: Seven gates: AND ($1$ only if all $1$), OR ($1$ if any $1$), NOT (flip), NAND (AND then NOT), NOR (OR then NOT), XOR ($1$ if odd number of $1$s, for $2$ inputs: inputs differ), XNOR (complement of XOR, equality detector). Memorise truth tables for $2$ inputs - everything else is composition.

NAND and NOR are universal: NOT from NAND by tying inputs ($NAND(A,A) = \bar{A}$), AND by NAND+NOT, OR by De Morgan ($A+B = \overline{\bar{A}\cdot\bar{B}}$ = three NANDs), and so on. CMOS naturally makes inverting gates (NAND/NOR/INV) faster and smaller than AND/OR, which is why libraries are NAND/NOR based.

VEDA Q2: design $4$-input NAND $Y = \overline{A\cdot B\cdot C\cdot D}$ using only $2$-input NANDs. Cascade method: $G1 = NAND(A,B) = \overline{AB}$. $G2 = NAND(G1,G1) = AB$. $G3 = NAND(G2,C) = \overline{ABC}$. $G4 = NAND(G3,G3) = ABC$. $G5 = NAND(G4,D) = \overline{ABCD}$. Five gates. Tree method also uses five: two ANDs (two NANDs each) plus final NAND. Minimum is five with strict $2$-input NANDs.

Exam drawing tips: label every intermediate ($AB$, $\overline{AB}$ etc.), show tied inputs clearly for inverters, and verify with $A=B=C=D=1$ (output must be $0$) and $A=0$ rest $1$ (output must be $1$).

subsections.title: XOR and XNOR - the odd/even detectors
content: $2$-input XOR: $A \oplus B = A'B + AB'$. $1$ when inputs differ. $3$-input XOR is $1$ for odd parity ($1$ or $3$ ones).
XNOR is complement: $A \odot B = AB + A'B'$. $1$ when inputs equal. Used in comparators (next sections).
XOR with $0$ passes through ($A \oplus 0 = A$), with $1$ inverts ($A \oplus 1 = \bar{A}$). This controllability is used in adder/subtractors.

subsections.title: NAND as NOT, AND, OR, NOR
content: NOT: $NAND(A,A) = \overline{A\cdot A} = \bar{A}$.
AND: $NAND$ then NOT: $AND(A,B) = NAND(NAND(A,B),NAND(A,B))$.
OR: invert inputs first: $OR(A,B) = NAND(\bar{A},\bar{B})$.
NOR: OR then NOT (four NANDs). In the exam, state the count if asked for minimum.

subsections.title: Why designers prefer NAND
content: In CMOS, NAND has series PMOS in parallel-friendly arrangement and is faster than NOR for wide inputs (electrons move faster than holes). Standard-cell libraries therefore NAND-heavy.
Any AND-OR network converts to NAND-NAND by double inversion + De Morgan. This is not just exam theory - synthesis tools do it daily.

quickRevision: 4-input NAND from 2-input NANDs: five gates (cascade or tree).
readingSections.companyNote: VEDA sample Q2 is exactly the 4-input NAND design. Draw cleanly with labels - presentation earns marks.

readingSections.title: 3. Minimization - Boolean Algebra and K-Maps
readingSections.quickSummary: Group 2^k adjacent ones in a K-map. Bigger groups kill more literals. Goal: fewest product terms with fewest literals.
content: Minimal SOP costs fewer gates and less delay. Two tools: algebra (Absorption $A+AB=A$, $A+A'B=A+B$, Consensus) for small proofs, K-map for $2$-$4$ variables in the exam hall.

K-map layout: $2$-var has $4$ cells, $3$-var has $8$, $4$-var has $16$. Order is Gray code ($00,01,11,10$) so neighbours differ by one bit - including wrap-around edges (left-right and top-bottom are adjacent). Diagonal cells are NOT adjacent.

Grouping rules: circle only $1$s (for SOP; $0$s for POS), groups must be rectangles of size $1,2,4,8,16$ (powers of $2$), overlap allowed and encouraged, every $1$ covered at least once, make groups as big as possible, use fewest groups. A group of $2^{k}$ kills $k$ literals. Don't-cares ($X$) can be taken as $1$ or $0$ whichever grows groups.

Example $F(A,B,C) = \sum(0,1,3,4,6)$ (VEDA Q3 function): K-map ones at $000,001,011,100,110$. Groups: $\bar{B}\bar{C}$ (cells $0,1,4$? check adjacency) - do systematically in the answer: one common minimal SOP is $F = \bar{B}\bar{C} + B'C? $ - actually minimise carefully: cells $0(000),1(001)$ pair gives $\bar{A}\bar{B}$? $000+001 = 00-$ = $\bar{A}\bar{B}$. Cells $0,4$: $000+100 = -00$ = $\bar{B}\bar{C}$. Cells $4,6$: $100+110 = 1-0$ = $A\bar{C}$. Cells $1,3$: $001+011 = 0-1$ = $\bar{A}C$. Essential prime implicants cover: minimal $F = \bar{B}\bar{C} + \bar{A}C + A\bar{C}$? Verify $m2(010)=0$: $\bar{B}\bar{C}=0$ (B=1), $\bar{A}C=0$ (C=0), $A\bar{C}=0$ (A=0): $0$. Good. $m5(101)=0$: $\bar{B}\bar{C}=0$ (B=0? $\bar{B}=1,\bar{C}=0$ so $0$), $\bar{A}C=0$ (A=1), $A\bar{C}=0$ (C=1): $0$. Good. $m7(111)=0$: all zero. Good. So $F = \bar{B}\bar{C} + C(\bar{A}+A\cdot?)$ - keep sum of three $2$-literal terms. MUX solution (next section) does not need this first, but minimised form helps gate-count questions.

subsections.title: Algebra shortcuts that replace big K-maps
content: $A + AB = A$. $A + \bar{A}B = A + B$. $AB + \bar{A}C + BC = AB + \bar{A}C$ (drop consensus).
$(A+B)(A+\bar{B}) = A$. $A\oplus B = A\bar{B} + \bar{A}B$.
Apply before drawing when you spot $X + \bar{X}Y$ or redundant third term.

subsections.title: Don't-cares and POS K-maps
content: Don't-care $X$ means output can be either (unused input combo or invalid BCD etc.). Include $X$ in a group only if it enlarges it.
POS K-map: group $0$s, read complements (variable uncomplemented where cell has $0$). Dual of SOP grouping.
If asked for minimum NOR-NOR or NAND-NAND, minimise to SOP then double-invert, or minimise POS for NOR-NOR.

subsections.title: Hazards glance (for timing-aware design)
content: Syllabus says design for functionality AND timing. A minimal SOP can glitch when one input flips between adjacent ones covered by different terms (static-1 hazard). Adding the consensus/redundant group removes it at the cost of one extra gate.
You will not be asked to draw hazard covers in prelims usually, but mentioning it in mains design answers shows timing awareness.

quickRevision: Group of 2^k kills k literals. Overlap freely.
Don't-cares help only if they grow a group.
readingSections.companyNote: K-map appears in both prelims (2-3 var) and mains (4-var with don't-cares). Practice Gray order until automatic.

readingSections.title: 4. Multiplexers and Demultiplexers (VEDA Q3 Inside)
readingSections.quickSummary: An n-select MUX is a 2^n-to-1 digitally controlled switch. Any n-variable function fits one MUX; (n-1) selects plus last variable on data pins is the exam favourite.
content: MUX equation ($4$-to-$1$ with selects $S1,S0$): $Y = \bar{S1}\bar{S0}D0 + \bar{S1}S0D1 + S1\bar{S0}D2 + S1S0D3$. DEMUX is the reverse: one input steered to $2^{n}$ outputs by selects, others $0$ (plus enable). A decoder with enable IS a DEMUX.

MUX is universal: $2$-to-$1$ MUX with $D0=0,D1=1$ is a buffer of $S$; $D0=1,D1=0$ is NOT; suitable constants give AND/OR. Any $n$-variable truth table maps directly: connect selects to variables, each data pin to the row's output ($0$/$1$). That uses $n$ selects.

Exam favourite uses $(n-1)$ selects and feeds the last variable (or its complement, $0$, $1$) to data pins - halves MUX size. VEDA Q3: $F(A,B,C) = \sum(0,1,3,4,6)$ on a single $4$-to-$1$ MUX. Two selects cover $B,C$; data pins get functions of $A$. Rows by $BC$: $BC=00$ has $m0(A=0)=1, m4(A=1)=1$: $D0=1$. $BC=01$ has $m1=1, m5=0$: $D1=\bar{A}$. $BC=10$ has $m2=0, m6=1$: $D2=A$. $BC=11$ has $m3=1, m7=0$: $D3=\bar{A}$. Wire $S1=B, S0=C, D0=1, D1=\bar{A}, D2=A, D3=\bar{A}$. Verify $ABC=011$: selects $11$ pick $D3=\bar{A}=1$: correct. $ABC=101$: selects $01$ pick $\bar{A}=0$: correct.

Implementation table method (fast in hall): list minterms per select combo; if both $0$: tie $0$; both $1$: tie $1$; only $A=0$ row is $1$: $\bar{A}$; only $A=1$ row is $1$: $A$. Choose any variable as the data variable - usually the MSB ($A$).

subsections.title: 2-to-1 MUX anatomy
content: $Y = \bar{S}D0 + SD1$. When $S=0$ pick $D0$, else $D1$.
Bigger MUXes cascade from $2$-to-$1$ ( Shannon expansion). An $8$-to-$1$ needs seven $2$-to-$1$s in tree, or two $4$-to-$1$ plus one $2$-to-$1$.
Enable ($E$): when $0$, output forced $0$ regardless. Active-low enables common in decoders.

subsections.title: DEMUX in one paragraph
content: $1$-to-$4$ DEMUX: $Y0 = \bar{S1}\bar{S0}Din, Y1 = \bar{S1}S0Din, Y2 = S1\bar{S0}Din, Y3 = S1S0Din$.
With $Din=1$ it is a decoder (selected output $1$). Routing, bus distribution and chip-select generation use it.
MUX (many-to-one, data selector) vs DEMUX (one-to-many, data distributor) - direction is the difference.

subsections.title: Design choices examiners reward
content: State selects and data mapping explicitly ($S1=B, S0=C, D0=1...$). Show the decomposition table. Verify two rows (one $1$, one $0$).
If only NAND gates allowed after MUX, keep MUX as block and convert surrounding inverters to NAND-tied.
Mention that any function of $B,C$ alone would need no $A$ on data pins - here $A$ is essential because rows differ.

quickRevision: (n-1) selects + last variable on data = minimum MUX.
DEMUX with Din=1 is a decoder.
readingSections.companyNote: VEDA sample Q3 is exactly the 4-to-1 mapping above. Reproduce the table, not just the final wiring.

readingSections.title: 5. Decoders, Encoders, Priority Encoders
readingSections.quickSummary: Decoder: n lines to 2^n minterms (one-hot). Encoder: reverse. Priority encoder breaks ties by fixed order plus a valid bit.
content: Decoder ($n$-to-$2^{n}$): exactly one output $1$ (active-high) for each input code; output $i$ IS minterm $m_{i}$. $2$-to-$4$ with $A,B$: $Y0=\bar{A}\bar{B}, Y1=\bar{A}B, Y2=A\bar{B}, Y3=AB$. With enable it demultiplexes. $3$-to-$8$ (74x138 style) has active-low outputs plus enables - read the bubbles carefully.
Any SOP function = decoder + OR: OR the minterm outputs. $F = \sum(0,1,3,4,6)$ = $3$-to-$8$ decoder with $Y0+Y1+Y3+Y4+Y6$ ORed. Useful when decoder already exists for address decoding.

Encoder ($2^{n}$-to-$n$): reverse, valid only if exactly one input is $1$. Priority encoder (e.g. $4$-to-$2$) resolves multiple ones by priority ($D3>D2>D1>D0$) and adds Valid $V=1$ if any input $1$. Truth table with $X$ (don't-care) rows: $D3=1$ gives $11$ regardless of lower bits.

Comparators belong nearby: $1$-bit equality $E = A\odot B = AB + \bar{A}\bar{B}$; $A>B$ is $A\bar{B}$; $A<B$ is $\bar{A}B$. Wider comparators cascade (e.g. $4$-bit 74x85 with $A>B, A=B, A<B$ cascade inputs).

subsections.title: Decoder as minterm generator
content: Each output is one minterm, so any function is a wired OR of outputs.
Active-low decoder outputs are maxterms instead - NAND them (or AND with bubbles).
Address decoding in memories is the industrial use: $n$ address lines pick one of $2^{n}$ rows.

subsections.title: Priority encoder truth table reading
content: $V = D3+D2+D1+D0$ (any request). Outputs encode highest active index.
$D3=1$: $Y=11$ irrespective of rest. $D3=0,D2=1$: $Y=10$. And so on. $0000$ gives $V=0$ (outputs don't care).
Keyboard encoders and interrupt controllers are priority encoders in silicon.

subsections.title: Seven-segment and code converters
content: BCD-to-seven-segment, binary-to-Gray, Gray-to-binary are fixed encoder/decoder ROMs - minimised SOPs per output.
Gray code changes one bit per step ($00,01,11,10$), which is why K-maps use Gray order and why Gray counters glitch less.

quickRevision: Decoder outputs are minterms. Encoder is the inverse.
readingSections.companyNote: Priority encoder with Valid bit is a favourite short-answer: draw table with X rows.

readingSections.title: 6. Adders, Subtractors, Comparators - Arithmetic Blocks
readingSections.quickSummary: Half adder: S=A xor B, C=AB. Full adder adds carry-in. Chain for ripple; lookahead for speed. Subtract via 2's complement.
content: Half adder (no carry-in): $S = A \oplus B$, $C = AB$. Full adder: $S = A \oplus B \oplus Cin$, $Cout = AB + Cin(A \oplus B) = AB + BCin + ACin$ (majority). Half subtractor: $D = A \oplus B$, $Borrow = \bar{A}B$. Full subtractor: $D = A \oplus B \oplus Bin$, $Bout = \bar{A}B + \bar{A}Bin + BBin$.

Ripple-carry adder chains $Cout$ to next $Cin$: simple, $O(n)$ delay. Carry-lookahead computes generates ($G=AB$) and propagates ($P=A\oplus B$ or $A+B$) in parallel: $C1 = G0 + P0C0$, $C2 = G1 + P1G0 + P1P0C0$, etc. Fast $O(\log n)$ at more gates. VEDA asks ripple delay ($n$ full-adder delays) vs lookahead concept, rarely full lookahead algebra.

Subtractor via adder: $A - B = A + \bar{B} + 1$ (2's complement). One control line $M$: $B \oplus M$ per bit plus $M$ as $Cin$ gives adder ($M=0$) / subtractor ($M=1$) in one circuit. Overflow for signed (previous topic) = $Cin \oplus Cout$ at MSB.

Comparators: $1$-bit $E = \overline{A \oplus B}$, $G = A\bar{B}$, $L = \bar{A}B$. $n$-bit compares MSB-first (like dictionary): check top bits, cascade down. IC 7485 pattern with $A>B, A=B, A<B$ cascading.

subsections.title: Full adder from two half adders
content: First half adds $A,B$: $S1, C1$. Second half adds $S1,Cin$: $S, C2$. $Cout = C1 + C2$.
This $5$-gate structure is the standard exam drawing. Label $S1$ intermediate.
XOR count: full adder uses two XORs - the slowest gates, setting critical path.

subsections.title: Ripple delay and why lookahead exists
content: Each full adder waits for carry: $n$-bit ripple takes about $n$ carry delays (plus sum XOR). $16$-bit ripple is ~$16$ gate stages.
Lookahead precomputes carries from $G,P$ - constant-ish depth. Costs more AND-OR fan-in. Modern adders (carry-select, Kogge-Stone) refine the trade-off.
Syllabus phrase design for timing points here: same function, different delay/area.

subsections.title: Comparator cascade logic
content: Compare MSB pair first. If differ, decision done. If equal, pass to next bits. Equality of words is AND of bitwise XNORs.
Magnitude comparator truth table for $2$ bits has $16$ rows - derive via MSB-first reasoning, not brute force.

quickRevision: HA: S=XOR, C=AND. FA: S=3-XOR, Cout=majority.
A-B = A + not-B + 1. M line makes adder/subtractor.
Ripple O(n) delay; lookahead precomputes via G/P.
readingSections.companyNote: Adder/subtractor derivations plus one ripple-vs-lookahead short answer cover this block's mains share.
